title: Altered Immune Response and Health Assessment in Nursing
introduction: An altered immune response—or hypersensitivity reaction—occurs when the immune system overreacts to foreign antigens or fails to maintain self-tolerance, causing host tissue damage or autoimmune disease[cite: 244, 375]. Effectively managing allergic reactions and broader clinical conditions depends on systematic nursing health assessment, integrating subjective health history with objective physical examination findings to build an accurate clinical database[cite: 378, 384, 385].
learningOutcomes: 5.1 Define hypersensitivity reactions and autoimmune disease, and classify the four types of hypersensitivity by immune mechanism and time sequence[cite: 244, 375, 376].

5.2 Compare Type I (anaphylactic/atopic), Type II (cytotoxic), Type III (immune-complex mediated), and Type IV (delayed cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reactions across antibodies, complement, mediators, clinical disorders, and skin tests[cite: 244, 376, 377, 378].
5.3 Perform a comprehensive nursing assessment for allergic patients, covering allergen categories, focused physical findings, and diagnostic tests[cite: 244, 378, 379, 380].
5.4 Explain the purpose of nursing health assessment, distinguish subjective from objective data, and describe the components of a general survey and adult health history[cite: 384, 385, 386].

5.5 Apply the eight critical symptom characteristics, Review of Systems sequence, and functional assessment tools (ADLs/IADLs, FICA, AUDIT/CAGE, and intimate partner violence screening)[cite: 387, 388, 393, 394, 395, 398].

content.heading: Hypersensitivity Overview and Type I (Anaphylactic & Atopic) Reactions
content.body: Hypersensitivity is an over-responsiveness of the immune system to an invading organism or foreign protein that damages the body's own tissues; when the body fails to recognize self-proteins and attacks self-antigens, the resulting conditions are termed autoimmune diseases[cite: 244, 375]. Hypersensitivity reactions are classified by antigen source, time sequence (immediate or delayed), and immunologic mechanism into four types: Types I, II, and III are immediate humoral reactions, whereas Type IV is a delayed cell-mediated reaction[cite: 244, 375]. Type I (IgE-mediated/anaphylactic) reactions occur in sensitized individuals exposed to exogenous allergens (pollen, food, drugs, dust)[cite: 244, 376]. On initial exposure, IgE antibodies bind to mast cells and basophils; on subsequent exposure, allergen cross-linking triggers degranulation and release of short-acting, reversible mediators—histamine, serotonin, slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis (SRS-A), eosinophil chemotactic factor of anaphylaxis (ECF-A), kinins, and bradykinin—without complement involvement[cite: 376]. Mediator effects include smooth muscle contraction, increased vascular permeability, vasodilation, hypotension, increased mucus secretion, and itching[cite: 244, 376]. Locally, mediators produce a diagnostic cutaneous wheal-and-flare reaction (pale edematous wheal surrounded by a red hyperemic flare, as in mosquito bites or allergy skin tests)[cite: 377]. Systemically, anaphylactic shock develops within minutes (e.g., after a drug injection or insect sting), progressing from local itching and edema to bronchoconstriction, airway obstruction, vascular collapse, rapid weak pulse, hypotension, dilated pupils, dyspnea, cyanosis, bronchial edema, angioedema, and potentially death without emergency care[cite: 244, 377]. Atopy represents an inherited tendency toward environmental allergen sensitivity, manifesting as allergic rhinitis, asthma, atopic dermatitis, urticaria, and angioedema[cite: 244, 377].

content.heading: Hypersensitivity Types II, III, and IV
content.body: Type II (cytotoxic and cytolytic) reactions involve direct binding of IgG and IgM antibodies to antigens on cell surfaces (such as RBC membranes or basement membranes), activating the complement cascade and neutrophils to destroy target cells (erythrocytes, platelets, leukocytes) rapidly via cytolysis or enhanced phagocytosis[cite: 244, 376, 377, 378]. Antigens include ABO blood groups, Rh factor, and drug haptens like chloramphenicol; characteristic disorders are ABO and Rh incompatibility transfusion reactions, autoimmune and drug-related hemolytic anemias, leukopenias, thrombocytopenias, erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn), and Goodpasture's syndrome, with no diagnostic skin test[cite: 376, 378]. Type III (immune-complex mediated) reactions occur when soluble extracellular fungal, viral, or bacterial antigens bind IgG and IgM to form small immune complexes that escape mononuclear phagocyte clearance and deposit in tissues or small blood vessels—commonly the kidneys, skin, joints, blood vessels, and lungs[cite: 376, 378]. Deposited complexes fix complement and recruit neutrophils via chemotactic factors, causing local or systemic inflammation in conditions like serum sickness, systemic lupus erythematosus, acute glomerulonephritis, and rheumatoid arthritis, with skin testing showing erythema and edema in 3 to 9 hours[cite: 376, 378]. Type IV (delayed hypersensitivity) is cell-mediated and requires neither antibodies nor complement: sensitized T lymphocytes directly attack intracellular or extracellular antigens or release cytokines (lymphokines) that attract macrophages, whose lysosomal enzymes cause most of the tissue destruction[cite: 244, 376, 378]. Reactions develop over 24 to 48 hours (as seen in the TB skin test showing erythema and edema), with clinical examples including contact dermatitis, bacterial/fungal/viral hypersensitivities, tumor rejection, and transplant rejection[cite: 244, 376, 378].

content.heading: Nursing Assessment and Diagnostics in Allergic Reactions
content.body: Comprehensive allergic nursing assessment integrates health history, physical examination, diagnostic workup, and allergen skin testing[cite: 378]. History explores family atopic predisposition, past and present allergies, seasonal patterns, recurrent respiratory problems, insect sting reactions, prescription and over-the-counter drug reactions, lifestyle and stress levels, a daily or weekly food diary, and home or workplace environmental exposures (pets, plants, air pollutants, floor coverings, heating/cooling systems)[cite: 244, 379]. Functional health patterns highlight malaise, food intolerance, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, fatigue, hoarseness, cough, dyspnea, mucosal itching/burning, and chest tightness[cite: 379]. Allergens fall into four categories: Inhalants (pollens, molds, spores, animal danders, house dust, mites), Contactants (plants, drugs, metals, cosmetics, dyes, fibers, chemicals), Ingestants (food, food additives, drugs), and Injectables (drugs, vaccines, insect stings)[cite: 244, 380]. A head-to-toe physical examination focuses on allergic sites: integumentary (urticarial rashes, wheal and flare, papules, vesicles, bullae, dryness, scaliness, scratches), eyes (conjunctivitis, lacrimation, rubbing/blinking, dark under-eye circles called 'allergic shiner'), ears (diminished hearing, immobile or scarred tympanic membranes, recurrent infections), nose (polyps, nasal voice, itchy nose, rhinitis, pale boggy mucosa, sneezing, nosebleeds, transverse nasal crease called 'allergic salute'), throat (continual clearing, swollen lips or tongue, palpable neck lymph nodes), and respiratory tract (wheezing, stridor, thick sputum)[cite: 244, 380]. Key diagnostic findings include eosinophilia in serum, sputum, or nasal/bronchial secretions, elevated serum IgE levels, positive skin tests, and abnormal chest or sinus X-rays[cite: 244, 380].

content.heading: Health Assessment in Nursing: Purpose, General Survey, and Health History
content.body: Health assessment is the systematic collection and analysis of subjective data (what the patient reports during history taking) and objective data (what the nurse observes via inspection, percussion, palpation, and auscultation plus laboratory studies) to build a clinical database[cite: 384, 385]. From this database, nurses formulate clinical judgments and nursing diagnoses—concise statements of actual or potential health concerns or levels of wellness[cite: 384, 385]. Nurses conduct physical assessments for five main purposes: developing baseline data for the nursing process, identifying and managing actual and potential patient problems, evaluating nursing care effectiveness, enhancing the nurse-patient relationship, and making clinical judgments[cite: 384, 385]. The General Survey evaluates overall health state, height, build, sexual development, weight, posture, motor activity, gait, dress, grooming, hygiene, body or breath odours, facial expression, affect, speech, and level of consciousness[cite: 385]. The complete adult health history captures seven sequential domains: (1) Biographic data (identity, demographics, usual and present occupation); (2) Reason for seeking care (a brief spontaneous statement recorded in quotation marks in the client's own words—never translated into a medical diagnosis—distinguishing subjective symptoms from objective signs); (3) Present health or history of present illness; (4) Past health; (5) Family history; (6) Review of systems; and (7) Functional assessment[cite: 386, 387].

content.heading: Symptom Characteristics, Past/Family History, and Review of Systems
content.body: For an ill patient, the chronological history of present illness must summarize eight critical symptom characteristics without interviewer bias: (1) Location (specific site, localized vs. radiating, superficial vs. deep), (2) Character or quality (descriptive terms or similes like 'tarry' stool or 'coffee-ground' vomitus), (3) Quantity or severity (objective measures or impact on daily activities rather than vague adjectives), (4) Timing (exact onset, duration, constant vs. intermittent frequency, remission/exacerbation cycles), (5) Setting (where the patient was and what triggered it), (6) Aggravating or relieving factors, (7) Associated factors in related body systems, and (8) Patient's perception ('what do you think it means?', alerting the nurse to underlying anxiety)[cite: 387, 388]. Past health covers specific childhood illnesses (avoiding vague labels like 'usual'), accidents/injuries, serious chronic diseases, hospitalizations, operations, obstetric history (recorded as Gravida, Term, Preterm, Abortions—spontaneous or induced—and Living), immunizations, last screening examinations, allergies (documenting both allergen and true allergic reaction rather than medication side effects), and all current prescription, over-the-counter (vitamins, aspirin, antacids, birth control), and herbal remedies[cite: 388, 389]. Family history maps age, health, and causes of death of blood relatives plus close household contacts (for communicable disease exposure) using a family tree or genogram[cite: 389, 390]. The Review of Systems (which may be combined with the physical exam) systematically screens body systems in head-to-toe order—skin, hair, nails, head, eyes, ears, nose/sinuses, mouth/throat, neck, breast, axilla, respiratory, cardiovascular, peripheral vascular, gastrointestinal, urinary, male/female genital, sexual health, musculoskeletal, neurologic, hematologic, and endocrine—paired with health promotion practices[cite: 390, 391, 392, 393, 398].

content.heading: Functional Assessment, Spiritual Tools, and Safety Screening
content.body: Functional assessment evaluates a person's self-care capacity across Activities of Daily Living (ADLs: bathing, dressing, toileting, eating, walking) and Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADLs needed for independent living: housekeeping, shopping, cooking, laundry, telephone use, managing finances), and may be structured around Gordon's (2002) functional health patterns or standardized instruments[cite: 393, 394]. Because functional topics are often private, they are best explored later in the interview once rapport is built[cite: 394]. Core domains include self-esteem/self-concept (education, finances, values), activity/exercise, sleep/rest, 24-hour nutrition/elimination recall, interpersonal support systems, and coping/stress management (asking about causes of stress and how the patient reacts)[cite: 394, 395, 397, 398]. Spiritual resources are assessed using the FICA framework: Faith (role of spirituality/religion), Influence (how beliefs shape health care), Community (religious congregation support), and Address (whether the client wants spiritual concerns addressed)[cite: 394, 395]. Personal habits screening quantifies tobacco in packs per day (PPD) and duration, evaluates alcohol use—which interacts adversely with medications and contributes to half of fatal traffic accidents—using the AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test) or CAGE (Cut Down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener) questionnaires, and assesses illicit drug use[cite: 395]. Finally, nurses screen environmental and occupational hazards and evaluate Intimate Partner Violence starting with open-ended questions ('How are things at home?', 'Do you feel safe?') before asking specific close-ended abuse questions if the client feels unsafe[cite: 395, 396].

inTextQuestions.question: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction occurs without the involvement of antibodies or complement, typically taking 24 to 48 hours to manifest?
inTextQuestions.answer: Type IV (delayed, cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction), which is mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes, cytokines, and macrophages (for example, contact dermatitis or a TB skin test)[cite: 244, 376, 378].

inTextQuestions.question: What are the clinical signs known as 'allergic shiner' and 'allergic salute' observed during a physical examination of an allergic patient?
inTextQuestions.answer: 'Allergic shiner' refers to dark circles under the eyes, and 'allergic salute' refers to a crease across the bridge of the nose from repeated rubbing/wiping[cite: 380].

inTextQuestions.question: In nursing health assessment, how does a 'symptom' differ from a 'sign'?
inTextQuestions.answer: A symptom is a subjective sensation felt and reported by the patient, whereas a sign is an objective abnormality detected by the examiner on physical examination or in laboratory reports[cite: 386].

saqs.question: Define hypersensitivity reaction and differentiate the four types of hypersensitivity in terms of antibodies/cells involved, complement involvement, and one clinical example each.
saqs.answer: Hypersensitivity is an over-responsiveness of the immune system to an invading organism or foreign protein that damages host tissues[cite: 375]. Type I (Anaphylactic): involves IgE on mast cells/basophils, no complement, e.g., allergic rhinitis, asthma, or anaphylactic shock[cite: 376, 377]. Type II (Cytotoxic): involves IgG/IgM binding cell-surface antigens, activates complement, e.g., ABO/Rh transfusion reaction or Goodpasture's syndrome[cite: 376, 378]. Type III (Immune-complex): involves IgG/IgM soluble immune complexes, activates complement, e.g., serum sickness, SLE, or rheumatoid arthritis[cite: 376, 378]. Type IV (Delayed): cell-mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes and macrophages with no antibodies or complement, e.g., contact dermatitis or transplant rejection[cite: 376, 378].

saqs.question: List the four categories of allergens with two examples each, and state four possible diagnostic findings in allergic/hypersensitivity reactions.
saqs.answer: The four allergen categories are: Inhalants (pollens, molds, animal danders, house dust, mites), Contactants (plants, metals, cosmetics, dyes, chemicals), Ingestants (foods, food additives, drugs), and Injectables (drugs, vaccines, insect stings)[cite: 244, 380]. Four diagnostic findings are eosinophilia (in serum, sputum, or nasal/bronchial secretions), elevated serum IgE level, positive skin tests, and abnormal chest or sinus X-rays[cite: 244, 380].

saqs.question: State five purposes for conducting a nursing health assessment and list the seven main categories of a complete adult health history.
saqs.answer: Five purposes are: (1) obtaining baseline data to expand the nursing database, (2) identifying and managing actual and potential patient problems, (3) evaluating the effectiveness of nursing care, (4) enhancing the nurse-patient relationship, and (5) making clinical judgments[cite: 384, 385]. The seven adult health history categories are biographic data, reason for seeking care, present health/history of present illness, past health, family history, review of systems, and functional assessment (including ADLs)[cite: 386].

saqs.question: List and briefly explain the eight critical characteristics that must be included when summarizing any symptom during the history of present illness.
saqs.answer: 1. Location (exact site, localized/radiating, superficial/deep); 2. Character or quality (specific descriptors or similes like burning, throbbing, or tarry); 3. Quantity or severity (measurable amount or impact on daily activities); 4. Timing (exact onset, duration, and constant vs. intermittent frequency); 5. Setting (location and activity when it began); 6. Aggravating or relieving factors; 7. Associated factors in related body systems; and 8. Patient's perception (what the patient believes the symptom means)[cite: 387, 388, 397, 398].

saqs.question: Distinguish between ADLs and IADLs in functional assessment, and explain how nurses screen for hazardous alcohol use and intimate partner violence.
saqs.answer: ADLs (Activities of Daily Living) cover basic self-care such as bathing, dressing, toileting, eating, and walking, whereas IADLs (Instrumental Activities of Daily Living) cover skills needed for independent living such as housekeeping, shopping, cooking, laundry, telephone use, and managing finances[cite: 393]. Hazardous alcohol use is screened by asking about frequency/quantity and applying the AUDIT or CAGE (Cut Down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener) questionnaires[cite: 395]. Intimate partner violence screening starts with open-ended questions ('How are things at home?', 'Do you feel safe?') followed by specific close-ended questions regarding physical, emotional, or sexual abuse if the patient feels unsafe[cite: 395, 396].
